signals.title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
- GLM-5.3 NVFP4, a quantized mixture-of-experts model with 753 billion parameters and 40 billion activated per token, requires about 464 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the 252 GB HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU.
- Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve the model through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint using tensor parallelism (TP=2), with each GPU holding and computing roughly half the weights.
- vLLM launches a distributed service across both Stations, enabling multi-token prediction, FP8 KV-cache storage, and prefix caching to maximize throughput under concurrent load.
- AIPerf benchmarks on the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset show overall output throughput peaking at 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16, then falling to 385.0 tokens per second at concurrency 32 with mean request latency of 453.5 seconds.

...

Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. 

The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

...

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

...

Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.

| Configured concurrency | Overall throughput (tok/s) | Mean request latency (s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean inter-token latency (ms/token) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 107.4 | 49.84 | 479.75 | 8.78 |
| 8 | 386.0 | 114.17 | 433.79 | 19.01 |
| 16 | 607.8 | 136.46 | 482.90 | 23.77 |
| 32 | 385.0 | 453.54 | 899.36 | 77.90 |

 Table 2. SPEED-Bench Coding results with prefix caching enabled, four MTP draft tokens per step, and an FP8 KV cache. Latency metrics are means over measured requests; warmup is excluded. TTFT measures time to the first token, which may be reasoning

Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.

signals.title: Neo4j’s rusty in-memory AI Agent graph database
signals.excerpt:
# Neo4j’s rusty in-memory AI Agent graph database 

 Chris Mellor Chris Mellor STORAGE EDITOR Blocks & Files editor 

 Published fri 13 Nov 2026 // 15:09 UTC 

Graph database supplier Neo4j’s Relate is an in-memory database built in Rust for AI Agents and Agentic Systems.

Relate brings multihop reasoning capabilities and GraphRAG to AI agents for more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. It’s engineered specifically for the execution loops of autonomous agents, natively auto-detecting agent harnesses and returning structured errors equipped with explicit retryable flags. These flags enable agents to handle exceptions and self-correct without custom parsing logic. Relate enforces a row cap combined with an in-band truncation marker to prevent context window saturation during large retrievals. This constraint ensures agents receive bounded and predictable payloads.

...

From seamless agent connectivity via MCP to multi-hop

...

Relate can run anywhere and is built from the ground up as a lightning-fast, in-memory database engineered specifically for the agent paradigm. Neo4j says that, with Relate, AI coding agents can create a database and start building applications in milliseconds.

It delivers sub-millisecond reads in memory to handle the high-frequency read/write cycles of agentic workloads. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity and execute graph traversals simultaneously. The database maintains strict transactional integrity using an in-memory engine with an optional fsync'd write-ahead log for durable stores. It provides native options to flush state to disk for long-term persistence. Relate is 100 percent openCypher and more than 97 percent GQL compliant out of the box.

Relate deploys seamlessly across Jupyter notebooks, web browsers, software containers, and edge devices, and runs natively wherever agents are at work. The database ships with built-in agent connectivity via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server and a dedicated CLI for direct execution. Relate also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints to provide drop-in support for existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks, and standard developer tooling.

Relate is open source software under the Apache 2.0 license, and is available now from here.

...

There are other in-memory databases built for AI agents:

- ArcadeDB (embedded mode) is a multi-model database (property graph + document + key-value + more) that can run fully embedded / in-process.Memgraph is shipping a high-performance open-source in-memory graph database written in C/C++ and designed for GraphRAG, AI memory, agentic AI, and real-time graph analytics. 
- FalkorDB is an in-memory graph database (sparse-matrix / GraphBLAS-based engine) focused on low-latency multi-hop queries for AI agents, knowledge graphs, and GraphRAG.
- Redis/Valkey (including Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey) is an ultra-low-latency in-memory key-value store that’s widely used as the short-term/working-memory layer for agents (session state, conversation buffers, and semantic caching.

signals.title: AWS Trainium Gets SGLang: 17 Models, Kimi-K3 on 3 Nodes - FourWeekMBA
signals.excerpt:
Amazon says SGLang-Neuron is “publicly available”, letting developers serve models and generate reinforcement-learning rollouts with the open-source SGLang engine on AWS Trainium chips “using the same SGLang interface you use today”. The SGLang team’s release post calls v0.1.0 “the first public release of SGLang’s backend for AWS Trainium”.

The release post lists 12 language models and 5 diffusion models, 17 in all by our count. Its largest deployment, Kimi-K3, runs across three Trainium3 nodes, and GLM-5.2 serves a 1M-token context. On GPT-OSS-120B, the post says a host-memory cache delivers 72% to 75% more output throughput.

...

AWS says the software is accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container and was “released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs”, Amazon’s chip unit. The SGLang post says it is “now open source and available in public preview”, co-developed by the SGLang team at RadixArk and Amazon Annapurna Labs, and that it “follows the closed beta” announced in October, about three weeks earlier by our arithmetic.

AWS describes it as an out-of-tree plugin: SGLang’s core keeps the API server, request handling and prefix caching, while the plugin implements “the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner”. AWS’s walkthrough uses a Trainium3 instance. The code is on GitHub.

...

The post says Kimi-K3 “is the largest deployment in this release”: “It runs on three Trainium3 nodes, one for prefill and two for decode”. It says GLM-5.2 serves 128K and 1M decode points, so the 1M-token point is about 7.8x the smaller one by our arithmetic, and that it runs on the public Neuron SDK 2.33.0.

...

The one throughput number in the post is for its hierarchical cache, which keeps evicted cache pages in host memory and loads them back on a later hit. “On GPT-OSS-120B at TP8 and 32K context, HiCache L2 delivers 72% to 75% more output throughput”, the post says.

...

Neither post compares Trainium serving speed or cost with Nvidia GPUs, and neither gives prices for running these models on Trainium. The 72% to 75% figure is for one model and one cache setting, measured by the developers, not independently.

signals.title: An Agent That Searches, Outlines, and Reads Entire Documents Outperforms Chunk-and-Embed Retrieval
signals.excerpt:
An Agent That Searches, Outlines, and Reads Entire Documents Outperforms Chunk-and-Embed Retrieval

# Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs An agent that searches, outlines, and reads entire documents outperforms chunk-and-embed retrieval

Published Nov 13, 2026

Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. 

What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. 

Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks.

How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro.

- The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges.
- Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s).
- Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read.

Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent)

Why it matters: Chunk-and-embed retrieval methods tend not to work well with documents in which the meaning of any given passage is not self-contained, such as financial reports, contracts, and regulatory filings. In such cases, letting a model search the whole document is more effective.

We’re thinking: Chunk-and-embed has its place, but letting agents write search queries can be a better approach. Beyond READ and RLM (covered in last week’s issue of The Batch), Search-R1 trains LLMs to reason their way through multi-turn searches, and IRCoT uses an LLM’s reasoning traces as a search query.

# llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem 

Published November 13, 2026 

 ggml-org

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

...

Today we release libraries `v1.0.0`, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

### Releases 

| Release | Library | Public header(s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| llama.cpp v1.0.0 - LLM inference in C/C++ | `libllama` | `llama.cpp/include/` |

The underlying machine learning engine of `llama.cpp` - `ggml` is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

signals.title: Azure VMs deliver inference performance in line with industry benchmarks | Microsoft Community Hub
signals.excerpt:
anhoward

Nov 13, 2026

## Azure ND GB200 v6 and ND GB300 v6 VMs deliver inference performance in line with bare metal and the published InferenceX reference. See the results, then meet the team at SC26.

Article contributed by: Dilip Patlolla, Wenqing Lan, Mingfeng Yang, Ali Vaziri, Aishwarya Prasad Tonpe, Huseyin Yildiz, Anshul Jain and Aditya Bhamidipati

Azure delivers AI inference performance on par with industry benchmarks. We evaluated Azure ND GB200 v6 and ND GB300 v6 virtual machines across multiple models and inference engines, comparing ND GB200 v6 VMs with matched bare-metal servers and ND GB300 v6 VMs with the published InferenceX reference. Across the tested configurations, Azure closely matched these baselines in throughput and latency, with selected ND GB200 v6 workloads showing gains over bare metal. These results demonstrate Azure’s ability to deliver responsive, high-throughput inference at performance levels consistent with industry reference systems.

...

### What we found on ND GB300 v6 

- Throughput: Essentially identical across the tested concurrency sweep. This is agreement across matched operating points, not just at a single peak-throughput setting. 

- Decode: Time per output token (TPOT), inter-token latency (ITL), and interactivity closely match. Once generation starts, Azure sustains a comparable streaming rate, with no meaningful steady-state decode penalty observed. 

- End-to-end latency: User-perceived response times remain operationally equivalent. This checks the complete request, not just first-token timing or the rate at which later tokens arrive. 

- First token: Typical time to first token (TTFT) matches. Some low-concurrency cases show wider variation, potentially reflecting first-request warm-up. These cases should be read alongside decode and end-to-end behavior, which remain closely aligned. 

- Precision and serving stack: FP4, FP8, Dynamo+SGLang, and Dynamo+TRT-LLM match, including tested multi-token prediction (MTP) variants. In plain terms, the result holds across the number formats (precisions) and serving software we tested.

...

The key takeaway is straightforward - Azure VMs can deliver industry-reference inference performance without an automatic VM performance discount. Across the tested workloads, Azure ND GB200 v6 VMs perform in line with bare-metal servers overall, while Azure ND GB300 v6 VMs closely track the published InferenceX reference. Together, these results support Azure VMs as a platform for responsive, high-throughput inference across the models, serving stacks, and scales evaluated.

signals.title: EnvOpt: Automatic Optimization of LLM Agent Environments
signals.excerpt:
Bespoke Labs, in collaboration with the University of Chicago and UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab, has introduced EnvOpt, a framework that automatically optimizes the file environment of LLM agents. According to the authors, it saves an average of 48% of execution costs across five benchmarks.

Compiled by Sergey Kostenchuk Published 2026-11-14 Updated 2026-11-15

Open the longform version with context, source trail, and what changed.

EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments Source

💻 EnvOpt: Optimizing LLM Agent Environments

Bespoke Labs, the University of Chicago, and UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab have released a framework that automatically improves an agent's "stationary environment"—files, data, and tools. Model parameters and the harness remain untouched, and across five benchmarks, the average savings on unseen tests is 48% while maintaining the pass rate.

🌍 The environment becomes a third optimization target alongside the model and the harness: the agent receives file indexes, SQLite table maps, and API hints in advance instead of searching from scratch. The effect transfers between models and harnesses.

👤 Agent costs can be reduced by changing not the model, but the delivery of data and tools: on AutomationBench, the optimization cost $150 and saved 77.5% of the execution costs for Claude Opus 4.8. The code is partially open on GitHub (itea1001/EnvOpt), and the environments are available on Hugging Face.

signals.title: Huawei Open-Sourced MACaQ, Which Quantized a 122B Model in 64 Minutes on 32.5 GB. Here Is the Weekend Test I'd Run on One GPU. | Solo Operator Stack
signals.excerpt:
# Huawei Open-Sourced MACaQ, Which Quantized a 122B Model in 64 Minutes on 32.5 GB. Here Is the Weekend Test I'd Run on One GPU.

Huawei's Computing Systems Lab in Switzerland open-sourced MACaQ (Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization) under Apache 2.0, with a paper submitted to arXiv on November 7. The headline claim is that it can "quantize a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes using just 32.5 GB of device memory." It outputs 2, 3 and 4-bit GGUF files for llama.cpp and W4A4 or weight-only checkpoints for vLLM. For anyone running local models, the question is not whether you need a 122B model. It is whether you can now quantize your own fine-tune on the GPU you already have.

...

The paper's abstract says the 122B run used "only 32.5GB GPU RAM." So this was a GPU run, and 32.5 GB fits on a single 48 GB workstation card. (It's just over the 32 GB on a consumer flagship, so read the number carefully.) That is the part worth noticing, if it holds up. Most of us download someone else's GGUF instead of making our own, partly because the tooling and hardware for doing it well feel out of reach.

What's missing matters too. Neither the README nor the abstract names the 122B model, and neither names the GPU. A 64-minute figure on an unnamed card is a hard number to plan around. I'd treat it as "a large model on one card in about an hour" and verify it on my own hardware.

On quality, the authors compare against MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ and claim lower perplexity, or the same best Llama-3-8B perplexity "with 11× less quantization time." That's a comparison against research methods, not against what most of us use. I found no head-to-head with llama.cpp's own importance-matrix quants or with AWQ in the material I read, and that is the comparison I care about.

...

The README has one concrete table I can use. On Qwen3.8-27B served through vLLM, BF16 perplexity is 2.8463 and MACaQ W4A4 is 2.8994. Prefill runs 2.33x faster and decode 2.58x faster than BF16. The lab's blog reports a 2.74x decode speedup in llama.cpp on the same model versus FP16.

...

Where I could be wrong: this is a week-old research release with an unnamed headline model and no comparison against the quants most people already use. It may turn out that llama.cpp's own quants are just as good for typical models, and MACaQ's edge only shows at W4A4 on vLLM. That's why the test above is a Saturday morning, not a migration.

signals.title: Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU
signals.excerpt:
Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.

The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.

LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.

...

Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.

This version is available in a separate repository. The self-hosting guide describes a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend accelerators from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.

...

The LongCat team reports 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, a benchmark that measures how well agents solve command-line tasks. Meituan lists Claude Opus 5 at 89.1, GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash at the top of the table with 90.6.

DeepSWE tests how well models fix bugs in real code repositories. Here LongCat-2.5 jumps from 9.7 to 64.6 points, placing it behind every other model in the table except Claude Opus 4.8, with Deepseek-V4.1-Flash leading at 74.2 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 72.7. The more recent Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol are not included in the table.

...

Terminal Bench v4.0, the harder variant, puts LongCat-2.5 at 38.5 points, slightly above GPT-5.6 Sol's 37.3 but well below Opus 5's 53.9. The model posts 91.9 on the web search benchmark BrowseComp, the highest score in the table, though Meituan ran this test in its own environment.

signals.title: End‑to‑End 4‑Bit Training - Thinking Machines Lab
signals.excerpt:
# End‑to‑End 4‑Bit Training

Jack Cook in collaboration with others at Thinking Machines Nov 13, 2026

...

Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. However, there is a tradeoff: fewer bits also mean fewer representable numbers, leading to more aggressive rounding. Lower-precision representations ultimately hurt accuracy by adding error to the calculations.

...

We manage this tradeoff through our use of three key numerical formats during training: BF16, MXFP8, and NVFP4. Each format’s precision is fixed, but its speed depends on the hardware being used. We train on NVIDIA’s Grace Blackwell Ultra platform, the GB300, which is designed to optimize matrix multiplications with NVFP4. Notably, NVFP4 is stored with 3.6x fewer bits than BF16, but it runs up to 6x faster on GB300s.

...

| Numerical format | Bits per value | GB300 PFLOPS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVFP4 | (4 × 16 + 8) ÷ 16 = 4.5 | 15 |
| MXFP8 | (8 × 32 + 8) ÷ 32 = 8.25 | 5 |
| BF16 | 16 | 2.5 |

The NVFP4 acceleration on GB300s is very useful in high-volume inference, where the tradeoff leans in favor of speed. But compared to BF16 and MXFP8, the format greatly increases quantization error. This error matters more at different stages of training, and the tradeoff must be considered for each one separately: forward and backward passes in pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), sampling and training in reinforcement learning (RL).

...

In training Inkling 2 Small, we made the following decisions:

- NVFP4 precision in the expert layers for forward passes, bolstered by a dedicated kernel.
- MXFP8 precision for backward passes with re-quantization and stochastic rounding, techniques for reducing gradient bias.
- Quantization techniques for accelerating GPU communications, which alleviated a bottleneck that surfaced after we sped up computation.

Inkling 2 Small is the largest model we are aware of that was trained end-to-end with a native 4-bit forward pass. We configure numerics in the same way from the start of pretraining through the final RL rollout. This makes training simpler and eliminates the need for calibration when a quantized checkpoint is delivered at the end of training. In our largest jobs, this recipe provides us with an 8% wall-clock speedup in pretraining and a 20% speedup in RL over full MXFP8 training. In this post, we explain the details that made this possible.

...

With our new NVFP4 matrix multiplications (GEMMs), our MoE layer’s forward pass should theoretically have gotten about three times faster compared to our MXFP8 implementation. But after reducing precision, we noticed we were running up against a bottleneck: communications during expert parallelism.

Since MoE layers are often very large, it is common to split up experts between different GPUs. When computing the MoE layer, a small router decides where each token should go, and tokens are then dispatched to the GPUs containing the routed experts. After completing the GEMMs, the computations of these routed experts are returned to the source GPU and combined to create the MoE layer’s final output. On an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system, the tokens will typically be sent over NVLink, which has a bandwidth of 900 GB/s in each direction. At the same time, the NVFP4 GEMMs will run at a speed of up to 15 PFLOPS. Dividing one by the other, each GPU could perform as many as 16,000 floating point operations in the time it takes to receive a single byte. Unless every byte that arrives brings at least that much computation with it, the Tensor Cores sit idle waiting on NVLink.

We found this imbalance created bottlenecks where either the MoE GEMMs were unable to execute because they were waiting to receive the dispatched tokens, or the following operation (in Inkling 2 Small, short convolutions) was unable to start because it was waiting to receive the combined tokens. During dispatch, we avoid this issue by dispatching tokens in NVFP4. Like TetraJet-v2 and Quartet II, our backward pass is computed using quantized — not high-precision — activations from the forward pass (note the input to the weight gradient, or WGRAD, computation in Figure 4), which reduces the amount of data sent over NVLink enough to alleviate the dispatch bottleneck. During combine, however, the output activations need to remain in higher precision (by default, BF16) to avoid impairing model performance.

We alleviate the communications bottleneck by quantizing the data transmitted during combine as well. We initially experimented with quantizing the resulting activations to MXFP8, but found that this impaired performance too much due to MXFP8’s poor representation of outlier values. Instead, we found that performing a 32-dimensional random Hadamard transform (RHT) and then quantizing to block-scaled S2F6, another 8-bit format, resulted in no measurable accuracy degradation during training.

signals.title: Google Just Open-Sourced the Engine Behind Six Million Queries a Second | AIWithGhost
signals.excerpt:
Training a model gets the glory. Serving it — answering millions of small requests every second — is where the bills pile up. Google has now open-sourced one of its sharpest answers to that problem: XSE, the XLA Serving Engine, a runtime that takes the Python interpreter out of the serving path completely.

The announcement landed on the Google Open Source Blog on November 5, from Oleg Shaldybin and Monica Song of Google's TPU software team. XSE is a general-purpose model export and inference runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, released under the Apache 2.0 license. And this is no research toy: inside Google, XSE already serves over six million queries per second, powering inference for Search, Google Ads, YouTube Shorts and parts of Gemini Omni.

## Train in Python, serve in C++ 

Google sums up the workflow in one line: "Train in Python, Serve in C++." Engineers keep writing model code in Python, usually with JAX handling the maths. When a model is ready, XSE's export API packages it as an "XLA SavedModel" holding the model's function in StableHLO, an intermediate representation the XLA compiler can work with. The XLA Serving Runtime then loads that package and runs it as compiled native code, with no interpreter sitting between the request and the answer.

...

The code and quick-start instructions live in the OpenXLA xla-serving repository on GitHub, and the runtime targets CPUs, GPUs and TPUs. PyTorch users are not left out for long, either: Google plans integration with TorchTPU, so PyTorch models can be exported for C++ serving on TPUs as well.

...

How fast is it? In Google's own tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of the best optimized Python server the company could build, while using a quarter of the memory. Read those numbers with the standard caution: they are vendor benchmarks, run on Google's workloads under Google's conditions, and nobody outside Google has replicated them yet. Still, removing an interpreter from a hot path almost always buys speed — and usually memory headroom too.

...

## Not a chatbot engine — and that is fine 

Some headlines will skip this part: XSE is not built for large-scale LLM inference. If you are serving a giant language model, Google itself points you towards vLLM or SGLang instead. XSE is a lightweight, one-shot inference engine aimed at the other end of the spectrum: smaller models, sharply defined tasks, one prediction per request, relentless volume.

signals.title: Huawei Quantizes 122B Model in 64 Minutes — AI Newsway
signals.excerpt:
A Huawei research group open-sourced MACaQ, an Apache 2.0 quantization toolkit that it says compressed the 122-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-122B-A10B to 4-bit in 64 minutes on one 96GB GPU, peaking at 32.5GB of memory.

...

A Huawei research group has open-sourced MACaQ, a quantization toolkit it says can compress a 122-billion-parameter model to 4-bit precision in 64 minutes while using only 32.5GB of GPU memory. The code went up on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, alongside a paper first posted to arXiv on Nov. 7, and the AI newsletter AI Weekly reported the release on Nov. 12. Every number below comes from the group's own paper and README; none has yet been reproduced outside the lab.

### Key takeaways

- MACaQ quantized Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, whose 16-bit weights take about 244GB, on a single 96GB GPU, and the 4-bit result fits back on that same card at 74GB.
- On Llama-3-8B, the authors report lower perplexity than the MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ methods, and say MACaQ matches their best scores in 11 times less quantization time.
- One codebase targets llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch, covering text, image, video and speech models.

...

MACaQ, short for Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization, converts both weights and activations to MXFP4, a 4-bit floating-point format, a setup known as W4A4. Most competing methods push their math transforms across neighboring layers to avoid any cost at inference time. MACaQ instead keeps a small scaling step and a block-Hadamard rotation inside each linear layer and runs them live.

That choice means each layer can be calibrated and quantized on its own, so only one layer has to sit on the GPU at a time while the rest wait in system memory. A refinement step the authors call Flip-Refinement then nudges individual 4-bit codes to neighboring values when that lowers the layer's output error.

In the paper, written by Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli, the 122B run used 512,000 calibration tokens. WikiText-2 perplexity rose from 5.06 at full precision to 5.14 after quantization.

...

The GitHub repository splits the work by backend: 2-, 3- and 4-bit GGUF files for llama.cpp, which also runs on CPUs; W4A4 or weight-only checkpoints for vLLM serving; and W4A4 for diffusion and speech models. A companion tool, MACaQ-R, refines existing GGUF files while keeping them compatible with standard llama.cpp.

Recipes target popular open models, including Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B, which became a common single-GPU choice after Alibaba open-sourced the family. Speed claims, however, depend on hardware with native 4-bit math; the paper's tests ran on an unnamed GPU with 96GB of memory.

The paper also lists limits. Because every layer is handled alone, errors cannot be compensated across layers. For mixture-of-experts models only the expert layers were quantized, and on a small 0.6B model the live transforms cost about 8% in speed.

...

The repository had 35 stars and 16 commits when AI Newsway checked it, so outside benchmarks are still thin. Huawei's own Ascend chips are only partly covered: W4A4 kernels sit in pending pull requests, and full-model runs still need integration with an Ascend inference runtime, the README says.

- Token output throughput rose 30% to 70% for 235B during traffic spikes.

For prefix caching:

- Effective cache capacity grew by an order of magnitude when MoE weights fill most of HBM.
- Average TTFT fell by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads.

signals.excerpt:
# Elasticsearch Unveils Serverless Vector Database, Streamlining RAG for Developers

Elastic has announced the release of Elasticsearch Vector Database, a new serverless product specifically engineered for large-scale vector search and AI applications. This offering aims to streamline the development process for RAG systems by providing an optimized database with pre-configured defaults, eliminating the need for extensive manual tuning. This development is significant for cloud and DevOps practitioners as it directly addresses the complexity and operational burden often associated with implementing vector search. Previously, building a vector-based application involved stitching together various components: document chunking, setting up embedding and reranking models, configuring indexes, and managing vector storage. Elasticsearch Vector Database automates much of this, allowing developers to bring their data and queries while Elastic handles the underlying infrastructure, embeddings, and tuning. This abstraction reduces time-to-market and lowers the specialized skill set required to deploy effective RAG solutions. The launch fits within a broader industry trend where vector databases are becoming a foundational component of AI infrastructure, particularly for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) with proprietary data. As RAG moves from experimental to mainstream, there's a clear demand for solutions that simplify its deployment and management. Other major database providers have also integrated vector capabilities, such as PostgreSQL with `pgvector` and MongoDB with Atlas Vector Search, indicating a shift towards making vector search a standard feature rather than a niche technology. The serverless model further aligns with cloud-native principles, offering scalability and cost-efficiency by paying only for consumed resources. In practice, this means developers can now more easily integrate advanced semantic search, AI agents, and contextual chatbots into their applications without becoming vector database experts. Practitioners should evaluate this offering for projects requiring rapid deployment of RAG capabilities, especially if they are already within the Elasticsearch ecosystem. The promise of predictable costs and out-of-the-box relevance, including hybrid search capabilities, makes it a compelling option. However, it's crucial to assess how well the pre-tuned defaults align with specific use case requirements and to understand the cost model for large-scale deployments, as performance and cost can vary significantly across different vector database solutions.

signals.title: IBM ships Granite 4.1 previews tuned to resist prompt injection - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
IBM ships Granite 4.1 previews tuned to resist prompt injection - DEV Community
Mikhail Savchenko
Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at inite.ai
# IBM ships Granite 4.1 previews tuned to resist prompt injection
IBM's Granite team has published LLMON, a markup language for language models, on the Hugging Face blog, together with two experimental models trained to read and write it: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. A GitHub repository with a toolkit, workflow examples and templates comes with them.
## What LLMON does
IBM's argument is that a model's context holds many kinds of material: system prompts, earlier turns, retrieved documents, tool output, output constraints and reasoning. Most of that structure is implicit or squeezed into formats such as JSON, which were built for parsers. IBM links this to brittleness in smaller models and to prompt-injection exposure.
LLMON marks each component with a meaningful tag. The delimiters are reserved special tokens in the vocabulary, so structure and ordinary text never share characters. Each block gets a short unique ID, and an execution block at the end states which instruction to run, which data it applies to, which requirements constrain it and where the answer goes. Content outside that execution block is still visible to the model but is treated as unreferenced material.
The preview models ship with their own chat template. You build the usual list of messages, name the parts of a turn (instruction, data, requirement) and flag each as executed or not. The template renders the markup. IBM also provides converters that turn JSON into LLMON and back without loss.
## The security claim
Indirect prompt injection hides a malicious instruction inside content the model is asked to process, such as a retrieved document or a tool response. IBM tested on the OPI benchmark, which plants injections in the data of standard NLP tasks. By its account, the other models it tried, open and closed, carried out injected instructions with high probability. The LLMON models avoided 47% more attacks than the best frontier model tested and 95% more than the best open-source model. IBM reports similar trends on the ASB and StruQ benchmarks.
There are limits. These benchmarks cover static injections, and IBM says attacks that unfold across many chat turns are still being worked on. It also describes the privilege rule (execution-block instructions are authoritative, input is only material) as learned behavior and not an enforced guarantee.
## Capability and training
IBM says general performance stays on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models across standard benchmark categories. The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints. Training re-serializes an ordinary instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON and adds decoy instructions and data that are left unbound. Reinforcement learning follows in five GRPO stages and a final DPO stage on a thousand preference pairs built from the model's own responses to injection attempts.
Teams can also define their own tags and tune a LoRA adapter on top. IBM demonstrates this on the ScienceWorld benchmark and points to a second notebook for tool-calling agents. Mellea, IBM's related project, supports LLMON natively.
## Status
IBM describes the release as an experimental preview for exploration and evaluation, not for production, and asks for feedback in GitHub Discussions.

signals.title: Cloudflare Open-Sources Kitesurf, Its Lightweight Browser Engine for AI Agents
signals.excerpt:
Cloudflare releases Kitesurf under Apache 2.0, offering a lightweight, Rust-based browser engine designed for AI agents and automation.

- By Bobby Borisov
- On November 14, 2026

Cloudflare has open-sourced Kitesurf, its lightweight browser engine built specifically for AI agents. The source code is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. It’s a browser engine in the sense that it can load websites, run JavaScript, and render pages, but it’s not a browser in the traditional sense (i.e., it doesn’t require Chromium or a full browser container).

First launched in August, Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. They expanded the offering in September with WebMCP support, additional APIs, and compatibility improvements. Developers can now inspect and modify the engine, run it locally, or deploy their own instances onto Cloudflare Workers rather than just using the company’s managed Browser Run APIs.

The engine is designed to reduce the compute required for browser automation. Instead of launching a full browser instance for each task, Kitesurf does the HTML parsing, CSS application, JS execution, and screenshot capture via a suite of Rust components compiled to WebAssembly.

Under the hood, Kitesurf uses Blitz for HTML parsing, DOM manipulation, and layout, and Stylo for CSS processing. JS execution is mostly via Cloudflare’s Dynamic Workers with the Boa JS engine as a WebAssembly-based fallback when required. It also uses the Linebender libraries for text layout and 2D graphics and Krilla for PDF generation.

...

Importantly, Kitesurf supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol so you can connect with existing automation tools, like Puppeteer, rather than having to switch to a completely different interface. That said, Cloudflare notes that Kitesurf doesn’t currently support all of the Chrome DevTools features.

Developers who’d like to test the project can clone the GitHub repo, install the dependencies, and run the engine locally via Wrangler. The dev server is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8787`, where you can view the pages via Chrome DevTools or connect automation clients to the CDP endpoint.

Kitesurf has to be deployed to a Cloudflare account on a Workers Paid plan as the engine uses Dynamic Workers to isolate each individual page. You don’t need the deployment for local development.

Cloudflare also notes that Kitesurf is still very much in the experimental stage and is under active development. The team is currently focused on improving web standards compliance, reliability, and resource usage and is keen to take any contributions from the community via GitHub.

# Neo4j introduces in-memory database to support agentic AI systems
By Express Computer on November 13, 2026
Graph database company **Neo4j** has introduced **Relate**, an open-source, in-memory database for **AI agents and agentic systems.** The announcement was made on November 12.
Written in Rust, Relate operates in-process, meaning it runs within an application rather than as a separate database server. It is released under the Apache 2.0 open-source licence.
The database uses the Cypher query language and includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and a command-line interface. AI coding agents can use it to create databases during application development.
Data is stored in memory by default, with an option to save it to disk for longer-term storage.
A June 2026 **Gartner report**, *Forecast Analysis: Agentic AI in DBMS, Worldwide*, estimates that machine users will account for 75% of database management system workloads by 2029, compared with 10% in 2025. It also projects that AI agents could generate 10 to 100 times more interactions than human users.
**Sudhir Hasbe**, President of Technology and Chief Product Officer at Neo4j, said Relate is “designed to run in-process for agent sandboxes and agent memory as well as on mobile or edge devices.”
